title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design Notification Service
summary: Design a multi-channel Notification Service that delivers email, SMS, push (mobile), and in-app notifications at the scale of ~1 B notifications/day.
objectives: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design a multi-channel Notification Service that delivers email, SMS, push (mobile), and in-app notifications at the scale of ~1 B notifications/day. The service supports templating with personalization, a per-user preference center (channel opt-in / opt-out, quiet hours, frequency caps), rate limiting (per-user, per-template, per-tenant), delivery tracking with retries and exponential backoff, and a unified API for upstream services (orders, social, billing). Focus on **multi-channel fan-out**, **template rendering**, **preference enforcement**, **rate limiting (token bucket)**, and **delivery with at-least-once semantics + idempotency**. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Multi-channel delivery**: email (SES / SendGrid), SMS (Twilio / Vonage), mobile push (FCM / APNs), in-app (WebSocket / long-poll to client apps).
- **Templates**: per-tenant templates with variables (`Hello {{name}}, your order #{{order_id}} shipped`), localized (10+ languages), versioned, A/B testable.
- **Preference center**: each user can opt in / out per channel per category (e.g., "promotional email off", "order updates SMS on"), set quiet hours (no notifications 22:00–07:00 local time), and set frequency caps (max 5 marketing emails / day).
- **Rate limiting**: per-user (no notification spam), per-template (don't send the same template > 10x / user / day), per-tenant (protect downstream providers — e.g., 100 emails / sec to SES).
- **Delivery tracking**: status (queued → sent → delivered → opened → clicked → bounced / failed / suppressed), with retries (exponential backoff, max 5 attempts).
- **Idempotency**: dedupe key on `(tenant_id, external_id)` prevents duplicate sends if upstream retries.
- **Batching**: combine multiple notifications into a digest (e.g., daily summary email).
- **Unsubscribe handling**: one-click unsubscribe in emails (List-Unsubscribe header), honoring within 1 minute.
- **Analytics**: delivery rates, open rates, click rates, bounce rates per tenant / template / channel.
- **Compliance**: CAN-SPAM (US), GDPR (EU), CASL (Canada) — opt-in records, suppression list, right-to-be-forgotten.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.95 % for the API (ingestion must not fail; delivery can be eventually consistent).
- **Latency**: API acknowledge p99 < 100 ms; first delivery attempt p99 < 30 s for push, < 5 min for email, < 60 s for SMS.
- **Scale**: 1 B notifications / day ≈ 12 k/s avg, 50 k/s peak (Black Friday, Prime Day).
- **Durability**: queued notifications never lost (Kafka with replication); at-least-once delivery.
- **Cost efficiency**: SMS is ~100× more expensive than email — prefer email when user has both.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Volume**: 1 B / day = ~12 k/s avg, ~50 k/s peak. Breakdown: email 70 % (700 M), push 25 % (250 M), SMS 4 % (40 M), in-app 1 % (10 M).
- **Storage**: 1 B notifications × 500 bytes (metadata + rendered body ref) × 90-day retention = ~45 TB. Rendered bodies stored in S3 / GCS, referenced by ID.
- **Kafka throughput**: 50 k/s × 2 KB avg event = 100 MB/s = 800 Mbps. Manageable with 6 brokers.
- **Provider rate limits**: SES ~100 emails/sec/account (raised via support ticket to 50 k/s); Twilio SMS ~10 k/s; FCM ~1 M/s; APNs ~10 k/s per cert.
- **Database writes**: 1 B inserts/day = ~12 k/s. Sharded Postgres or DynamoDB handles this easily.
- **Redis**: rate-limit state for 1 B users × 4 channels × 10 templates = 40 B keys × 64 bytes = ~2.5 TB hot. Redis Cluster with ~500 GB usable per shard × 5 shards × 3 replicas.

### Scope
In scope: ingestion API, template engine, preference + rate-limit enforcement, multi-channel fan-out, retries + idempotency, delivery tracking, unsubscribe / suppression. Out of scope: marketing campaign orchestration (separate design), ML-based send-time optimization, rich push media handling.

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Ingestion API** (REST + gRPC): receives `POST /notifications` from upstream services (orders, billing, social). Validates, applies idempotency check, enqueues to Kafka. 2. **Kafka** topic `notifications`: partitioned by `tenant_id + user_id` (so all notifications for one user land on the same partition, preserving order for that user). 3. **Pre-processor worker**: consumes Kafka, fetches user preferences, evaluates rate limits, applies quiet-hours check, routes to per-channel Kafka topics or drops (if suppressed). 4. **Template Service**: renders templates with variables + locale; stores versions in Postgres, rendered output cached in Redis. 5. **Preference Service**: per-user preferences (channel opt-ins, quiet hours, frequency caps), per-tenant defaults. 6. **Rate Limiter**: token-bucket per (user, channel, template), implemented in Redis with Lua scripts for atomicity. 7. **Suppression List**: users who unsubscribed / bounced / marked spam; checked before every send. 8. **Channel Dispatchers** (one per channel): - **Email Dispatcher**: batches emails, calls Amazon SES / SendGrid API, tracks bounces via SNS webhook. - **SMS Dispatcher**: calls Twilio / Vonage API, tracks delivery receipts. - **Push Dispatcher**: calls FCM (Android) / APNs (iOS) APIs, handles token invalidation. - **In-App Dispatcher**: pushes to user's WebSocket connection (or queues if offline). 9. **Delivery Tracker**: receives status callbacks from providers, updates `notification.status`, triggers retries on transient failures. 10. **Retry Queue**: dead-letter queue (Kafka topic) for notifications that exhausted retries; alerts ops. 11. **Analytics Pipeline**: Kafka → Flink → ClickHouse / Redshift for delivery metrics. 12. **Storage**: Postgres (sharded by `user_id`) for notifications + preferences + templates; Redis for hot cache + rate limits; S3 for rendered bodies. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Upstream[Upstream Services
orders, billing, social] --> API[Ingestion API
idempotency check] API --> K1[(Kafka: notifications
partitioned by user)] K1 --> PP[Pre-Processor Worker] PP --> PS[Preference Service] PP --> RL[Rate Limiter
Redis Lua token-bucket] PP --> SL[Suppression List] PP --> TS[Template Service
render + localize] PP --> K2E[(Kafka: email)] PP --> K2S[(Kafka: sms)] PP --> K2P[(Kafka: push)] PP --> K2I[(Kafka: inapp)] K2E --> ED[Email Dispatcher
SES / SendGrid] K2S --> SD[SMS Dispatcher
Twilio / Vonage] K2P --> PD[Push Dispatcher
FCM / APNs] K2I --> ID[In-App Dispatcher
WebSocket] ED --> SES[(Amazon SES)] SD --> TW[(Twilio)] PD --> FCM[(FCM / APNs)] ID --> WS[User WebSocket] ED -. callback .-> DT[Delivery Tracker] SD -. callback .-> DT PD -. callback .-> DT DT --> PG[(Postgres: notifications
status, retries)] DT --> RQ[(Retry Queue / DLQ)] DT --> AN[Analytics: Kafka -> Flink -> ClickHouse] style PP fill:#ffe4b5 style DT fill:#b5ffe4 style RL fill:#ffd5d5 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Upstream | | Ingestion | | Kafka | | Services |----->| API |----->|notifications| | (orders, | | idempot. | | (partitioned| | billing) | | + validate| | by user) | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----+-----+ | v +---------------+ | Pre-Processor | | Worker | +-------+-------+ | +------------------+------------------+ | | | v v v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ |Preference | | Rate | |Suppressn | | Service | | Limiter | | List | | (opt-ins, | | (Redis | | (unsub / | | quiet hr,| | Lua token| | bounce / | | freq cap)| | bucket) | | spam) | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | | | +------------------+------------------+ | v +---------------+ | Template | | Service | | (render + i18n)| +-------+-------+ | +------+------+------+------+ v v v v +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ |Kafk| |Kafk| |Kafk| |Kafk| |a: | |a: | |a: | |a: | |eml | |sms | |psh | |inp | +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+ | | | | v v v v +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ |Email| | SMS | |Push | |InApp| |Disp | |Disp | |Disp | |Disp | +--+--+ +--+--+ +--+--+ +--+--+ | | | | v v v v +--+--+ +--+--+ +--+--+ +--+--+ | SES | |Twilio| |FCM/| |WS | | | | | |APNs| |conn| +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ | | | | +--callback---callback--+ v +-------------+ | Delivery | | Tracker | | (status, | | retries) | +------+------+ | +---------------+---------------+ v v v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Postgres | | Retry / | | Analytics | | (notif | | DLQ | | (Kafka -> | | status) | | | | Flink -> | | | | | | ClickHse)| +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Ingest**: Upstream service calls `POST /notifications` with `{tenant_id, user_id, template_id, channel, variables, external_id}`. API computes dedupe key `sha256(tenant_id + external_id)`, checks Redis `idempotency:{key}` — if exists, returns 200 OK with the existing notification_id (no duplicate). Otherwise enqueues to Kafka `notifications` topic and returns 202 Accepted with new notification_id. 2. **Pre-process**: Pre-processor consumes the event, fetches user preferences from Preference Service (cached 60 s in Redis), checks: (a) is the channel enabled for this category? (b) is the user in quiet hours? (c) is the user on the suppression list? (d) does the rate-limit token bucket have a token? If any check fails, the notification is dropped (with `status=dropped` and a reason). If all pass, the template is rendered and the notification is routed to the appropriate per-channel Kafka topic. 3. **Dispatch**: The channel dispatcher consumes from its Kafka topic, calls the provider API (SES / Twilio / FCM), and records the provider's message ID. 4. **Track**: Provider callbacks (SES SNS, Twilio webhook, FCM delivery receipts) hit `POST /callbacks/{provider}` → Delivery Tracker updates `notification.status = delivered | bounced | failed`. On transient failure (5xx, throttled), the notification is re-enqueued with exponential backoff (1 min, 5 min, 15 min, 1 h, 4 h). On permanent failure (bounce, invalid token), it's marked `failed` and added to the suppression list. 5. **Analytics**: Status changes stream to Kafka → Flink aggregates per template / tenant / channel → ClickHouse for dashboards.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Postgres (sharded by `user_id`) — `notifications`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE notifications (
    notification_id  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_id           BIGINT NOT NULL,
    template_id       VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    channel           VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,    -- email | sms | push | inapp
    external_id       VARCHAR(128),            -- upstream dedupe key
    variables         JSONB,
    rendered_body_ref VARCHAR(256),            -- s3://bucket/key
    status            VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,    -- queued | rendered | sent | delivered | bounced | failed | dropped | suppressed
    provider          VARCHAR(32),             -- ses | twilio | fcm | apns
    provider_msg_id   VARCHAR(128),
    attempt_count     INT DEFAULT 0,
    next_attempt_at   TIMESTAMP,
    created_at        TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at        TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_id)            -- idempotency
);
CREATE INDEX ON notifications (user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON notifications (tenant_id, template_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON notifications (status, next_attempt_at) WHERE status IN ('queued','retrying');
```

**Postgres — `templates`** (per-tenant, versioned)
```sql
CREATE TABLE templates (
    template_id    VARCHAR(64),
    tenant_id      BIGINT,
    version        INT,
    channel        VARCHAR(16),
    locale         VARCHAR(10),               -- en_US, fr_FR, ...
    subject        TEXT,
    body           TEXT,                      -- with {{variables}}
    is_active      BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at     TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (template_id, tenant_id, version, locale)
);
```

**Postgres — `user_preferences`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE user_preferences (
    user_id           BIGINT,
    tenant_id         BIGINT,
    category          VARCHAR(32),            -- marketing | transactional | security
    email_enabled     BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    sms_enabled       BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    push_enabled      BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    inapp_enabled     BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    quiet_hours_start TIME,                   -- e.g., '22:00'
    quiet_hours_end   TIME,                   -- e.g., '07:00'
    quiet_hours_tz    VARCHAR(32),            -- 'America/New_York'
    daily_cap_email   INT DEFAULT 10,
    daily_cap_sms     INT DEFAULT 5,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, tenant_id, category)
);
```

**Postgres — `suppression_list`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE suppression_list (
    user_id      BIGINT,
    tenant_id    BIGINT,
    channel      VARCHAR(16),
    reason       VARCHAR(32),    -- unsubscribe | bounce | spam_complaint | manual
    bounced_email VARCHAR(255),
    created_at   TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, tenant_id, channel)
);
```

**Redis**
```
# Rate limit tokens (token bucket)
KV   rl:{user_id}:{channel}:{template_id}:{day}     # token count, TTL 25h
KV   rl:{user_id}:{channel}:daily_cap                # daily count, TTL 25h
KV   rl:{tenant_id}:provider:{provider}              # tenant-level provider rate

# Idempotency
KV   idem:{sha256(tenant_id + external_id)}         # notification_id, TTL 24h

# Preference cache
KV   pref:{user_id}:{tenant_id}                     # JSON, TTL 60s

# Template render cache
KV   tpl:{template_id}:{version}:{locale}:{vars_hash}  # rendered body, TTL 1h

# Provider callback tracking
KV   cb:{provider}:{provider_msg_id}                # notification_id, TTL 7d
```

### Indexes
- `notifications (user_id, created_at DESC)` — "show me my notifications".
- `notifications (tenant_id, template_id, created_at DESC)` — analytics by template.
- `notifications (status, next_attempt_at)` — retry worker scans this.
- `suppression_list (user_id, tenant_id, channel)` — pre-send check.
- `templates (template_id, tenant_id, version, locale)` — render lookup.

### Storage Choice
- **Postgres (sharded by `user_id`)** for notifications + preferences + templates: ACID transactions essential for status updates (a half-committed retry is a bug); sharding by user_id co-locates a user's notifications on one shard.
- **Redis Cluster** for rate-limit tokens, idempotency keys, preference cache, template render cache: sub-ms reads, atomic Lua scripts for token-bucket.
- **Kafka** for the async pipeline (ingestion → pre-process → dispatch): decouples write throughput (50 k/s) from provider rate limits (SES 100/s/account).
- **S3** for rendered bodies (HTML email content): cheap, durable, referenced by URL.
- **ClickHouse** for analytics: columnar, fast aggregations on billions of notification events.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
### API Design
```
# Ingestion (idempotent)
POST /api/v1/notifications
  headers: X-Tenant-Id, Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
  body: {
    "user_id": 12345,
    "template_id": "order_shipped",
    "channel": "email",                // or "auto" for preference-based selection
    "category": "transactional",
    "variables": {"order_id": "X123", "name": "Alice"},
    "external_id": "order-X123-ship-email",   // idempotency key
    "locale": "en_US"
  }
  resp: 202 Accepted { "notification_id": "uuid", "status": "queued" }
         200 OK { "notification_id": "uuid", "status": "duplicate" }   // idempotent

# Status query
GET  /api/v1/notifications/{id}
  resp: { "status": "delivered", "provider": "ses", "provider_msg_id": "...", "attempts": 1 }

# Preference center (user-facing)
GET  /api/v1/users/me/preferences
PUT  /api/v1/users/me/preferences
  body: { "marketing": {"email_enabled": false, "sms_enabled": false},
          "quiet_hours": {"start": "22:00", "end": "07:00", "tz": "America/New_York"} }

# Unsubscribe (one-click from email)
GET  /api/v1/unsubscribe?token=<signed_jwt>&channel=email&category=marketing
  -> adds to suppression_list, redirects to confirmation page

# Provider callbacks (webhooks)
POST /api/v1/callbacks/ses      # SNS webhook for bounces/opens
POST /api/v1/callbacks/twilio   # SMS delivery receipts
POST /api/v1/callbacks/fcm      # Push delivery receipts
```

### Key Algorithms

**1. Idempotency.** Upstream services may retry (network blip, timeout). Without dedup, a user could get the same "Order shipped" email twice. Solution: the upstream provides an `external_id` per logical notification. The Ingestion API computes `key = sha256(tenant_id + external_id)` and checks Redis `idem:{key}`. If present, returns 200 OK with the existing `notification_id` (idempotent — no duplicate send). If absent, generates a new `notification_id`, writes `idem:{key} = notification_id` with TTL 24h, enqueues to Kafka. Race condition: two concurrent requests with the same `external_id` could both pass the check. Mitigation: use Redis `SET key value NX EX 86400` (atomic set-if-not-exists) — only one request wins; the other gets the existing value.

**2. Token-bucket rate limiting (Redis Lua).** Multiple dimensions: per-user per-channel daily cap, per-user per-template daily cap, per-tenant per-provider rate (to respect SES limits). Implementation: a Lua script atomically checks all dimensions and decrements tokens:
```lua
-- KEYS[1] = user_daily_cap, KEYS[2] = user_template_cap, KEYS[3] = tenant_provider_rate
-- ARGV[1] = now_ms, ARGV[2] = window_ms, ARGV[3] = max_user, ARGV[4] = max_template, ARGV[5] = max_tenant
local u = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])  -- atomic increment
if u == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 86400) end
if u > tonumber(ARGV[3]) then return 0 end   -- user daily cap exceeded
local t = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2])
if t == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[2], 86400) end
if t > tonumber(ARGV[4]) then return 0 end   -- template cap exceeded
local p = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[3])
if p == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[3], 1) end   -- per-second tenant rate
if p > tonumber(ARGV[5]) then return 0 end   -- tenant rate exceeded
return 1   -- all checks passed, send
```
The Lua script runs atomically in Redis (single-threaded), so no race conditions.

**3. Channel preference + cost-aware routing.** When `channel = "auto"`, the service picks the best channel: (a) check user preferences (which channels enabled for this category); (b) check suppression list (skip suppressed channels); (c) prefer the cheapest channel that's enabled: in-app (free) > push (free) > email (cheap, $0.0001) > SMS (expensive, $0.05). For transactional / security notifications (e.g., 2FA code), prefer the highest-priority channel the user has (SMS > push > email) to ensure delivery.

**4. Quiet hours.** Each user has `quiet_hours_start`, `quiet_hours_end`, `quiet_hours_tz`. The pre-processor checks: is the user's current local time within quiet hours? If yes and the notification is non-urgent (marketing), hold it until quiet hours end (schedule with a delay queue). If urgent (security alert), bypass quiet hours.

**5. Template rendering.** Templates use Jinja2 / Handlebars syntax with `{{variable}}`. Rendered output is cached in Redis (`tpl:{template_id}:{version}:{locale}:{vars_hash}`, TTL 1h) — if the same template + variables is rendered again (e.g., password reset email sent to many users with same text), the cache hit avoids re-rendering. Variables are validated against a schema (no missing vars, no XSS in HTML). Locale fallback: `fr_CA` → `fr_FR` → `en_US` → default.

**6. Retries with exponential backoff.** On transient failure (provider 5xx, throttled), the notification is re-enqueued with `next_attempt_at = now + backoff(attempt)`. Backoff schedule: 1 min, 5 min, 15 min, 1 h, 4 h (jittered ±20 %). After 5 attempts, mark `failed` and move to DLQ. The retry worker scans `WHERE status = 'retrying' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` every 10 s. Permanent failures (hard bounce, invalid phone number) are not retried — they go straight to `failed` and the user is added to the suppression list.

**7. Suppression list enforcement.** Before every send, check `suppression_list (user_id, tenant_id, channel)`. Reasons: (a) **unsubscribe** — user clicked unsubscribe; (b) **hard bounce** — email address doesn't exist; (c) **spam complaint** — user clicked "Mark as spam" in their client; (d) **manual** — admin suppressed. The list is cached in Redis for 5 min. Adding to suppression is immediate (within 1 click); removing is via the preference center (only for `unsubscribe` reason, not `bounce` — bounced emails need re-verification).

```python
# notification_service.py — multi-channel fanout with idempotency, rate limit, retry
import hashlib, time, json, threading
from collections import defaultdict

class RedisMock:
    """Atomic Lua-style operations simulated in Python."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.kv = {}; self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def set_nx(self, key, value, ttl):
        with self.lock:
            if key in self.kv: return False
            self.kv[key] = (value, time.time() + ttl); return True
    def get(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            v = self.kv.get(key)
            if not v: return None
            if time.time() > v[1]: del self.kv[key]; return None
            return v[0]
    def incr_with_ttl(self, key, ttl):
        with self.lock:
            v = self.kv.get(key)
            if not v or time.time() > v[1]:
                self.kv[key] = (1, time.time() + ttl); return 1
            new = v[0] + 1; self.kv[key] = (new, v[1]); return new

class PostgresMock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.notifications = {}; self.preferences = {}; self.suppression = defaultdict(set)
        self.templates = {}; self.callbacks = []
    def insert_notification(self, n):
        self.notifications[n["id"]] = n
    def update_status(self, nid, status, provider=None, msg_id=None):
        n = self.notifications[nid]
        n["status"] = status; n["provider"] = provider; n["provider_msg_id"] = msg_id
        n["updated_at"] = time.time()
    def is_suppressed(self, user_id, tenant_id, channel):
        return (user_id, tenant_id, channel) in self.suppression
    def suppress(self, user_id, tenant_id, channel, reason):
        self.suppression[(user_id, tenant_id, channel)] = reason

class IngestionAPI:
    def __init__(self, redis, pg): self.r = redis; self.pg = pg
    def post_notification(self, tenant_id, user_id, template_id, channel,
                          category, variables, external_id, locale="en_US"):
        key = hashlib.sha256(f"{tenant_id}:{external_id}".encode()).hexdigest()
        idem = self.r.get(f"idem:{key}")
        if idem:
            print(f"  [api] duplicate (external_id={external_id}) -> returning {idem}")
            return idem, "duplicate"
        nid = f"notif-{key[:12]}"
        if not self.r.set_nx(f"idem:{key}", nid, ttl=86400):
            return self.r.get(f"idem:{key}"), "duplicate"
        n = {"id": nid, "tenant_id": tenant_id, "user_id": user_id,
             "template_id": template_id, "channel": channel, "category": category,
             "variables": variables, "external_id": external_id, "locale": locale,
             "status": "queued", "attempt_count": 0, "created_at": time.time()}
        self.pg.insert_notification(n)
        print(f"  [api] accepted {nid} (template={template_id}, channel={channel})")
        return nid, "queued"

class TemplateService:
    def __init__(self, redis, pg): self.r = redis; self.pg = pg
    def register(self, template_id, body, channel="email"):
        self.pg.templates[template_id] = body
    def render(self, template_id, variables, locale="en_US"):
        body = self.pg.templates.get(template_id, "{{name}}: {{message}}")
        rendered = body
        for k, v in variables.items():
            rendered = rendered.replace(f"{{{{{k}}}}}", str(v))
        return rendered

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, redis): self.r = redis
    def check(self, user_id, channel, template_id, tenant_id, provider):
        # Per-user per-channel daily cap
        u = self.r.incr_with_ttl(f"rl:u:{user_id}:{channel}:daily", ttl=86400)
        if u > 10:
            print(f"  [rl] user daily cap exceeded ({u} > 10)")
            return False
        # Per-user per-template daily cap
        t = self.r.incr_with_ttl(f"rl:u:{user_id}:{template_id}:daily", ttl=86400)
        if t > 3:
            print(f"  [rl] template cap exceeded ({t} > 3)")
            return False
        # Per-tenant per-provider rate (per second)
        p = self.r.incr_with_ttl(f"rl:t:{tenant_id}:{provider}", ttl=1)
        if p > 5:
            print(f"  [rl] tenant provider rate exceeded ({p} > 5/s)")
            return False
        return True

class PreProcessor:
    def __init__(self, redis, pg, template_svc, rate_limiter):
        self.r = redis; self.pg = pg; self.tpl = template_svc; self.rl = rate_limiter
    def process(self, n):
        # 1. Check suppression list
        if self.pg.is_suppressed(n["user_id"], n["tenant_id"], n["channel"]):
            self.pg.update_status(n["id"], "suppressed")
            print(f"  [pp] {n['id']} suppressed (user on suppression list)")
            return None
        # 2. Check preferences (mock: assume enabled)
        # 3. Check quiet hours (mock: assume not quiet)
        # 4. Rate limit
        provider = {"email": "ses", "sms": "twilio", "push": "fcm", "inapp": "ws"}[n["channel"]]
        if not self.rl.check(n["user_id"], n["channel"], n["template_id"],
                              n["tenant_id"], provider):
            self.pg.update_status(n["id"], "rate_limited")
            print(f"  [pp] {n['id']} rate-limited")
            return None
        # 5. Render template
        rendered = self.tpl.render(n["template_id"], n["variables"], n["locale"])
        n["rendered_body"] = rendered
        self.pg.update_status(n["id"], "rendered")
        print(f"  [pp] {n['id']} rendered: '{rendered[:60]}...'")
        return n

class ChannelDispatcher:
    def __init__(self, pg, provider_name, fail_rate=0.0):
        self.pg = pg; self.provider = provider_name; self.fail_rate = fail_rate
    def send(self, n):
        n["attempt_count"] += 1
        # Simulate provider call with random failure
        import random
        if random.random() < self.fail_rate:
            self.pg.update_status(n["id"], "failed", self.provider, None)
            print(f"  [disp:{self.provider}] {n['id']} send FAILED (attempt {n['attempt_count']})")
            return False
        msg_id = f"{self.provider}-msg-{int(time.time()*1000)}"
        self.pg.update_status(n["id"], "sent", self.provider, msg_id)
        print(f"  [disp:{self.provider}] {n['id']} sent (msg_id={msg_id})")
        return True

class DeliveryTracker:
    def __init__(self, pg): self.pg = pg
    def on_callback(self, provider, msg_id, event):
        # Find notification by provider_msg_id
        for nid, n in self.pg.notifications.items():
            if n.get("provider_msg_id") == msg_id:
                if event == "delivered":
                    self.pg.update_status(nid, "delivered")
                    print(f"  [track] {nid} delivered")
                elif event == "bounced":
                    self.pg.update_status(nid, "bounced")
                    self.pg.suppress(n["user_id"], n["tenant_id"], n["channel"], "bounce")
                    print(f"  [track] {nid} bounced -> user suppressed")
                elif event == "opened":
                    self.pg.update_status(nid, "opened")
                    print(f"  [track] {nid} opened")
                return

class RetryWorker:
    def __init__(self, pg, dispatcher):
        self.pg = pg; self.disp = dispatcher
    def retry_failed(self):
        for nid, n in self.pg.notifications.items():
            if n["status"] == "failed" and n["attempt_count"] < 3:
                backoff = [60, 300, 900][n["attempt_count"] - 1]
                print(f"  [retry] {nid} attempt {n['attempt_count']+1} (backoff {backoff}s)")
                self.disp.send(n)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    redis = RedisMock(); pg = PostgresMock()
    tpl_svc = TemplateService(redis, pg)
    tpl_svc.register("order_shipped", "Hi {{name}}, order #{{order_id}} shipped!")
    tpl_svc.register("promo", "Hi {{name}}, 50% off everything today!")

    api = IngestionAPI(redis, pg)
    rl = RateLimiter(redis)
    pp = PreProcessor(redis, pg, tpl_svc, rl)
    email_disp = ChannelDispatcher(pg, "ses", fail_rate=0.3)
    tracker = DeliveryTracker(pg)

    print("=== 1. Send a notification ===")
    nid1, _ = api.post_notification(
        tenant_id=1, user_id=100, template_id="order_shipped",
        channel="email", category="transactional",
        variables={"name": "Alice", "order_id": "X123"},
        external_id="order-X123-ship")

    n1 = pg.notifications[nid1]
    if pp.process(n1):
        email_disp.send(n1)

    print("\n=== 2. Idempotency (duplicate external_id) ===")
    nid2, status = api.post_notification(
        tenant_id=1, user_id=100, template_id="order_shipped",
        channel="email", category="transactional",
        variables={"name": "Alice", "order_id": "X123"},
        external_id="order-X123-ship")  # same external_id
    print(f"  Result: nid={nid2}, status={status} (should be 'duplicate', same id)")

    print("\n=== 3. Rate limit (send same template 4 times) ===")
    for i in range(4):
        nid, _ = api.post_notification(
            tenant_id=1, user_id=100, template_id="promo",
            channel="email", category="marketing",
            variables={"name": "Alice"},
            external_id=f"promo-{i}")
        n = pg.notifications[nid]
        pp.process(n)

    print("\n=== 4. Delivery callback (delivered) ===")
    # Find a sent notification
    for nid, n in pg.notifications.items():
        if n["status"] == "sent" and n.get("provider_msg_id"):
            tracker.on_callback("ses", n["provider_msg_id"], "delivered")
            break

    print("\n=== 5. Bounce -> suppression ===")
    # Manually send another and simulate bounce
    nid_b, _ = api.post_notification(
        tenant_id=1, user_id=200, template_id="order_shipped",
        channel="email", category="transactional",
        variables={"name": "Bob", "order_id": "Y456"},
        external_id="order-Y456-ship")
    n_b = pg.notifications[nid_b]
    if pp.process(n_b):
        email_disp.send(n_b)
        if n_b.get("provider_msg_id"):
            tracker.on_callback("ses", n_b["provider_msg_id"], "bounced")

    print("\n=== 6. Try to send to suppressed user (should be suppressed) ===")
    nid_c, _ = api.post_notification(
        tenant_id=1, user_id=200, template_id="promo",
        channel="email", category="marketing",
        variables={"name": "Bob"},
        external_id="promo-bob-1")
    n_c = pg.notifications[nid_c]
    pp.process(n_c)  # Should be suppressed

    print("\n=== Summary ===")
    for nid, n in pg.notifications.items():
        print(f"  {nid}: status={n['status']}, attempts={n['attempt_count']}, "
              f"provider={n.get('provider')}")
```

Running this demonstrates: idempotent ingestion (duplicate `external_id` returns same notification_id), rate limiting (4th promo email is dropped), delivery tracking (callback updates status), bounce → suppression (Bob is suppressed after bounce), and suppression enforcement (subsequent sends to Bob are dropped).

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Ingestion throughput**: 50 k/s peak writes. Kafka with 12 partitions handles this easily; the Ingestion API is stateless and scales horizontally behind a load balancer.
- **Pre-processor throughput**: each notification requires ~4 Redis lookups (preference, suppression, rate-limit, idempotency) + 1 template render. At 50 k/s, that's 200 k Redis ops/s — Redis Cluster with 5 shards handles this. Pre-processor workers scale by Kafka consumer group; 50 workers at 1 k/s each.
- **Provider rate limits**: SES at 100 emails/sec/account is the binding constraint for high-volume tenants. Mitigation: multiple SES accounts per tenant (round-robin), request limit increases via AWS support, batch emails (10 per SES API call), and pre-warm the queue during off-peak hours for marketing blasts.
- **Callback flood**: a Black Friday email blast to 10 M users generates 10 M delivery callbacks (open / click / bounce) within hours. Mitigation: async webhook handlers, Kafka buffer, batch writes to Postgres (100 per INSERT), aggregate counters in Redis.
- **Redis hot keys**: a single tenant with a popular template can create a hot rate-limit key. Mitigation: shard the counter across `rl:t:{tenant}:{provider}:0..15` and sum at read time.
- **APNs / FCM token invalidation**: ~5 % of push tokens become invalid per month (user uninstalls app, gets new device). Mitigation: on invalid-token callback, mark the device as inactive in the device registry; nightly job cleans up.

### Caching Strategy
- **L1 (Redis)**: preferences (TTL 60 s), suppression list (TTL 5 min), template renders (TTL 1 h), idempotency keys (TTL 24 h), rate-limit counters (TTL matches window).
- **L2 (Postgres)**: source of truth. Cache misses fall through with a single SELECT.
- **L3 (S3 + CDN)**: rendered HTML email bodies (large, immutable).

### Failure Modes
- **Provider outage** (SES down): emails queue in Kafka; retries with exponential backoff. After 1 hour of consecutive failures, alert ops and switch to backup provider (SendGrid) for affected tenants. No data loss — Kafka retains events for 7 days.
- **Kafka partition leader failure**: ISR replicas elect a new leader within seconds; consumers resume. At-least-once delivery means a few notifications may be sent twice — idempotency at the provider level (SES MessageId dedup) catches duplicates.
- **Redis cluster failure**: rate-limit checks fail open (allow the send) rather than fail closed (drop the notification) — better to risk over-sending than to lose transactional notifications. Suppression list and preferences fall back to Postgres (slower but functional).
- **Postgres shard failure**: synchronous replica promotes within 30 s. Notification status updates are blocked during failover but ingestion continues (queued in Kafka).
- **Callback webhook spoofing**: providers sign their webhooks (SES SNS, Twilio) with HMAC; the Delivery Tracker verifies the signature before processing.
- **Poison pill message**: a malformed notification event in Kafka can crash a pre-processor worker. Mitigation: catch all exceptions in the consumer, log + skip (move to DLQ). Don't let one bad event block the partition.
